title: Shloka 136
subtitle: Consecration, the quelling of demons, and being itself

namas.translation: She has been formally initiated and holds to the observance, bound by her own vow as a sacrificer is bound.
The sons of Diti are put down by her whenever they press too far.

children.gloss: a son of Diti, a demon

namas.gloss: Bringing All Worlds Under Her Sway
namas.translation: Every region there is falls under her control.

compound.gloss: she who subjugates all the worlds

namas.translation: Whatever anyone is after, she is the one who supplies it.

compound.gloss: she who grants all desired ends

namas.translation: She is Sāvitrī, at once the verse addressed to the sun that every twice-born recites and the goddess that verse invokes.

namas.gloss: Whose Form Is Being, Consciousness And Bliss
namas.translation: She is made of three things that turn out to be one: that she is, that she knows, and that she is glad.

morphology.note: The suffix -in does the possessive work, so saccidānandarūpa is the compound and rūpiṇī the taddhita formed on it. The familiar bahuvrīhi rendering, she who has being, consciousness and bliss for her form, is no less sound.

compound.gloss: having being, consciousness and bliss as her own form

children.vigraha: sac ca cic ca ānandaś ca

commentary.meaning: The verse begins with a single three-syllable word that changes the register of everything around it. Dīkṣitā means consecrated, initiated, placed under vow: the technical term for a person who has entered a rite and is bound by its observances until the rite is finished. The previous verse called her satyasandhā, one whose engagements hold; this one opens by saying she is under engagement. What follows reads as the content of the vow. She quiets the demons, she brings every world under her control, and she gives whatever is sought — the three works of a consecrated power, moving from suppression through mastery to unconditional generosity. The fifth name identifies her with the verse that every initiated brahmin recites at dawn, which closes a circle, since it is by receiving that verse that a person becomes initiated at all. And the sixth abandons the ritual frame entirely for the plainest metaphysical formula the tradition possesses: being, consciousness, bliss. That name is the seven hundredth of the thousand, and it reads like a summit reached rather than an item on a list.
commentary.history:
Dīkṣā is one of the oldest technical words in Indian religion, and its Vedic sense is not the modern one. Before a soma sacrifice the patron underwent a consecration that the Brāhmaṇa literature describes without embarrassment as a gestation: he was installed in a hut treated as a womb, wrapped, girdled, made to keep his fists clenched like a foetus, put on a diet of milk, and at the end of it said to be born a second time, now qualified to sacrifice. The dīkṣita is not simply someone who has been given something; he is someone put under constraint who cannot leave it until the work is done.

Tantric usage keeps the constraint and adds a transmission. Dīkṣā in these schools is the initiation by which a teacher conveys a mantra and the eligibility to use it; the traditional etymology, repeated widely in the tantric literature, splits the word into a giving and a destroying — what confers knowledge and consumes the residue of past action. Calling the goddess dīkṣitā admits two readings the tradition does not separate: she is the reality present in every consecration, so that the transmission is finally hers rather than the teacher's; and she is herself under vow.

Daityaśamanī reads differently once dīkṣitā is in place. Daityas are the sons of Diti, opposed in the old cosmology to the Ādityas. The verb is what to notice. Śamanī is from √śam, whose primary sense is to become quiet and whose causative means to pacify — but Vedic ritual language also uses it as the standard euphemism for killing the sacrificial animal, and the officiant who performs the killing is the śamitṛ, the quieter. The word sits on the seam between calming and slaughter. Placed immediately after a name meaning consecrated, it lets the first line be heard as a sacrificial sequence: the patron takes the vow, and then the victim is quieted. Reading battle as sacrifice is old and widespread, and the campaign against Bhaṇḍāsura in which this hymn is embedded is told in exactly that key.

Sarvalokavaśaṅkarī brings in a further technical vocabulary. Tantric ritual manuals classify the applied uses of mantra into six acts, and though the lists vary in wording they consistently begin with pacification and subjugation — śānti and vaśīkaraṇa. Śamanī and vaśaṅkarī answer to the first two in canonical order, unlikely to be accidental in a hymn this saturated with ritual terminology. Vaśīkaraṇa is a coercive rite performed to bend another person's will. The hymn takes the technique out of the practitioner's hands: it is not that she can be used to subjugate the worlds, but that the worlds are already subject to her.

Sarvārthadātrī reverses the direction. Artha is elastic in Sanskrit — an object, a purpose, wealth, a meaning — and it is the second of the four human aims. After two names about power exercised over others, this one describes power given away.

Sāvitrī is a name with three distinct referents. It is first the verse of the Ṛgveda addressed to Savitṛ, the impeller, which an initiated twice-born recites at dawn and dusk throughout life; because that verse is composed in the twenty-four-syllable gāyatrī metre it is usually called the Gāyatrī, though strictly gāyatrī names the metre and sāvitrī the verse. It is second the goddess personifying that verse. And it is third the heroine of the episode in the third book of the Mahābhārata, who followed Yama when he took her husband's life and argued him out of it by holding the god of death to his given word — worth remembering one verse after satyasandhā. The first sense closes a loop: the sāvitrī is conferred at the upanayana, the initiation that makes a boy twice-born, so the name at the end of the line names what makes the dīkṣita of the first line possible.

Saccidānandarūpiṇī is the formula of Vedānta. The three words are Upaniṣadic separately, and the Taittirīya Upaniṣad's definition of brahman as truth, knowledge and the infinite is its clear ancestor, but the fused compound saccidānanda is a later crystallisation, current in Vedāntic and tantric writing rather than in the earliest texts. The hymn attaches rūpiṇī, having that as her form — so what for the strictest Advaita characterises an impersonal absolute is here predicated of somebody with a name, an army and a city. Three verses earlier the hymn called her free of being and non-being alike. Here it calls her being. The two are not reconciled anywhere in the text, and the tradition has preferred to keep both.
commentary.practice:
The verse is symmetrical in a way that makes it easy to hold: three syllables, five, eight in the first line; five, three, eight in the second. Both lines end on an eight-syllable name, so the verse falls into two matched halves. The second line is also heavily alliterative on s — sarvārtha, sāvitrī, saccidānanda — continuing the run of s-initial names begun in the previous verse.

Dīkṣitā opens with the conjunct kṣ, which is one sound rather than two in practice: the tongue makes the velar closure and releases directly into a retroflex sibilant. The word is three syllables, dī-kṣi-tā, long, short, long. Daityaśamanī begins with the diphthong ai, which is a full long vowel and not the quick glide of English eye; the vṛddhi of dai- marks daitya as a patronymic, son of Diti, so the length carries grammatical information.

Sarvalokavaśaṅkarī has a nasal worth attention. Written with the velar ṅ before k, it is the sound at the end of English sing. The name is often printed with an anusvāra instead — vaśaṃkarī — and the two spellings represent the same pronunciation. The nāmāvalī form given in the present edition, sarvalokavaṃśakaryai, has the nasal in the wrong place and has lost the vaśaṅ- of the stotra reading; the expected dative is sarvalokavaśaṅkaryai, and that is what most printed nāmāvalīs give.

Saccidānandarūpiṇī rewards being taken apart, because the assimilations that make it look forbidding are entirely regular. The elements are sat, cit and ānanda. A final dental t before an initial palatal c becomes c, which gives sac-cit; then cit before a vowel voices its final to d, giving cid-ānanda. The doubled cc in the middle is nothing but a t that has taken on the colour of its neighbour. Say sac-ci-dā-nan-da-rū-pi-ṇī with the doubled consonant held and the ṇ of rūpiṇī retroflex; an ordinary n there is the commonest error in the name.

In the archanā form, where each name takes the dative and is followed by namaḥ, this verse is nearly uniform: five of the six names are ī-stems and contract the long ī to y before the ending. Daityaśamanyai, sarvalokavaśaṅkaryai, sarvārthadātryai, sāvitryai, saccidānandarūpiṇyai. Only the first is an ā-stem, dīkṣitāyai. Sarvārthadātrī is a feminine agent noun on the -tṛ suffix that also gives dātā, giver.

What the verse asks is a particular attentiveness to its first word, because everything else depends on how dīkṣitā is heard. Taken as a description of a status she confers, the verse is about her power. Taken as a description of a vow she has entered, the verse is about her obligation, and the three names that follow become the terms of that obligation rather than a display of capacity. The second reading is the one that makes sense of the movement from quelling to giving. Either way, the name at the end resets the scale. Having spent five names in the vocabulary of ritual and power, the hymn finishes by saying she is what is, what knows, and what is glad — and then goes on to the next verse without comment.

crossReferences.iast: tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi | dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt ||
crossReferences.translation: May we take to ourselves that desirable radiance of the god Savitṛ, who shall impel our thoughts.
crossReferences.relevance: This is the sāvitrī the name refers to: not a goddess with a story but a single verse, twenty-four syllables long, transmitted at initiation and recited twice daily for the rest of a life. Identifying the goddess with it is a strong claim, since it makes her the content of the one utterance that constitutes brahmin religious identity. It also explains why the name sits in a verse that opens with dīkṣitā, because the sāvitrī is precisely what is conferred at the initiation that makes a person twice-born.

crossReferences.deva: सत्यं ज्ञानमनन्तं ब्रह्म । यो वेद निहितं गुहायां परमे व्योमन् । सोऽश्नुते सर्वान्कामान्सह ब्रह्मणा विपश्चितेति ॥
crossReferences.iast: satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma | yo veda nihitaṃ guhāyāṃ parame vyoman | so'śnute sarvān kāmān saha brahmaṇā vipaściteti ||
crossReferences.translation: Brahman is the real, knowledge, the endless. Whoever knows it as set down in the hidden place, in the furthest sky, obtains all desires together with brahman, the discerning.
crossReferences.relevance: The Upaniṣadic ancestor of saccidānandarūpiṇī. The three terms here are the real, knowledge and the endless rather than being, consciousness and bliss, and watching the one triad become the other is the best short lesson in how Vedāntic formulae were assembled after the Upaniṣads rather than found ready-made in them. The passage also bears on sarvārthadātrī two names earlier: it promises all desires, but only as a by-product of knowing, and to one who is not asking for them.

crossReferences.source: Devī Māhātmya, chapter 5 (the refrain of the hymn to the goddess as universally present; verse numbering varies between editions)
crossReferences.deva: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु शक्तिरूपेण संस्थिता । नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमो नमः ॥
crossReferences.iast: yā devī sarvabhūteṣu śaktirūpeṇa saṃsthitā | namas tasyai namas tasyai namas tasyai namo namaḥ ||
crossReferences.translation: The goddess who abides in all beings in the form of power — to her homage, to her homage, to her homage, homage upon homage.
crossReferences.relevance: The corrective to reading sarvalokavaśaṅkarī as conquest. The Devī Māhātmya's long litany insists that she is already resident in every being as the faculty by which it does anything at all, which means that bringing the worlds under her sway is not an operation performed on them from outside but a statement about what they are made of. It is also why a name drawn from the vocabulary of coercive tantric ritual can sit in a devotional hymn without embarrassment.

Read the treatment of the dīkṣā in the third book, where the consecration is worked out as a gestation, and dīkṣitā will stop reading as a vague honorific and start reading as a description of somebody who is confined, silent and not yet free to leave.

references.note: A short, unromantic account of the ṣaṭkarmāṇi with translated ritual instructions. It is the quickest way to understand what vaśīkaraṇa actually was as a practice, and reading it makes the sahasranāma's redeployment of the term visible as a deliberate move rather than a coincidence of vocabulary.

references.note: The Sāvitrī episode in a translation that does not sentimentalise it. What is striking on a close reading is how much of the story is argument: she wins by out-talking Yama and holding him to boons he granted carelessly, which is a very different kind of heroism from the one later retellings assign her.

references.note: For the Taittirīya passage quoted above together with Śaṅkara's commentary on it. Śaṅkara's discussion of how three nouns in apposition can define a single reality without dividing it is the argument that later stands behind saccidānanda, and it is more careful than most summaries of it.

references.note: Worth consulting on dīkṣitā in particular, since this is the kind of name where the traditional commentary supplies ritual detail that no dictionary will give and no modern translation preserves. It also shows how the exegesis handles a name like sāvitrī that has three separate referents, none of which it is willing to give up.
